setting: A short lecture in a marine biology class about coral bleaching and rising sea temperatures.
narrator_intro: Listen to part of a talk in a marine biology class.

talk.speaker: speaker1
talk.text: Coral reefs look like rocky gardens, but living coral animals build those structures over time.

talk.speaker: speaker1
talk.text: Many corals depend on tiny algae that live inside their tissues and share energy from photosynthesis.

talk.speaker: speaker1
talk.text: When ocean water stays unusually warm, that partnership breaks down—a process called bleaching.

talk.speaker: speaker1
talk.text: The coral turns pale because it loses the colorful algae, and without them it can starve.

talk.speaker: speaker1
talk.text: Some reefs recover if temperatures cool quickly, but repeated heat waves raise the risk of mass die-offs.

talk.speaker: speaker1
talk.text: Bleaching also weakens habitat for fish that communities rely on for food and tourism.

talk.speaker: speaker1
talk.text: Scientists track surface temperatures with satellites and send divers to count bleached colonies on site.

talk.speaker: speaker1
talk.text: Protecting reefs means cutting greenhouse gases and reducing local stress from pollution and overfishing.

talk.speaker: speaker1
talk.text: In short, coral health is an early warning system for how oceans respond to a warming climate.

talk.speaker: speaker1
talk.text: Next week we’ll examine case studies from the Great Barrier Reef and the Caribbean.

narrator_outro: Now get ready to answer the questions.

questions.narrator_text: What is the talk mainly about?

options.A: How to build artificial beaches for tourists
options.D: Coral bleaching and how ocean warming threatens reefs

questions.explanation: The professor explains bleaching, warm water stress, and why reef health signals climate impacts.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing C—satellites are only mentioned as a monitoring tool.

questions.narrator_text: According to the professor, why do many corals need algae?

options.A: The algae share energy from photosynthesis with the coral
options.B: The algae scare away all sharks
options.C: The algae turn seawater into fresh water

questions.explanation: He says algae live inside coral tissues and share energy from photosynthesis.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing B or C—those are not mentioned.

options.A: Coral loses its algae, turns pale, and may starve
options.C: Ocean water freezes around the reef
options.D: Fish paint the coral with new colors

questions.explanation: Bleaching is when coral loses colorful algae, turns pale, and can starve.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing B—bleaching is harmful, not helpful growth.

questions.narrator_text: What does the professor imply about protecting reefs?

options.A: Only tourism matters; climate action does not
options.B: Reefs need no protection if satellites exist
options.C: Divers should stop visiting oceans entirely
options.D: Both global emissions cuts and local reductions in pollution and overfishing matter

questions.explanation: He links greenhouse gas cuts with reducing local stress from pollution and overfishing.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing A—he treats climate and local stress together.
